title: Walks Covering Every Open Cell
statement:
You get a grid of integers:

  • 1 is the start cell (exactly one),
  • 2 is the finish cell (exactly one),
  • 0 is an open cell,
  • -1 is a wall.

A walk moves one cell up, down, left or right at a time. Count the walks from the start to the finish that step on every non-wall cell exactly once, including the start and the finish. The walk ends as soon as it reaches the finish.

examples.why: From the start you reach the finish after one open cell, and the other open cell is left behind. No walk covers all four.
Only down, right, up, right, down covers all six cells. Starting to the right traps the bottom-left cell.
Snake along the rows, or snake along the columns. Every other walk strands a cell.

hints: The grid has at most 20 cells. Trying every walk is acceptable if you stop dead ends early.
Count the non-wall cells first. A walk is valid exactly when it reaches the finish having stepped on that many cells.
Depth-first search from the start: mark the current cell as visited, try the four neighbours, then unmark it on the way back. At the finish, count 1 only if no cell is left.

explain.intuition:
There is no shortcut formula for covering walks; this is a Hamiltonian-path count, and the small grid is the hint that exhaustive search is expected. The job is to search cleanly: one walk at a time, never stepping on a cell twice, and undoing each step when you back out of it.

Keep a counter of how many cells are still unvisited. When the walk lands on the finish, it is a valid walk only if that counter says the finish was the last cell. Landing on the finish early is a dead end, because a walk cannot pass through the finish and come back.
steps: Scan the grid: find the start and count every cell that is not a wall.
Run dfs(r, c, left), where left counts the unvisited cells including (r, c).
If (r, c) is the finish, return 1 when left == 1, otherwise 0.
Otherwise mark (r, c) as a wall, sum dfs over the in-bounds non-wall neighbours with left − 1, then restore the cell and return the sum.
pitfalls: Forgetting to restore the cell after exploring it. Later walks then see a wall that is not there.
Continuing past the finish. Reaching it early must end that branch with 0.
Leaving the start or the finish out of the cell count, which makes every answer 0 or off by one step.

complexity.time: O(3^k) where k is the number of open cells

solutions.title: DFS that copies the visited set
solutions.idea: Carry a fresh set of visited cells into every recursive call. Simple to reason about, but every step pays to copy the set.

solutions.title: In-place backtracking with a remaining count
solutions.idea: Mark the current cell as a wall while exploring, restore it afterwards, and carry the number of cells still to visit.

followups: Memoise on (cell, set of visited cells) as a bitmask. When does that beat plain backtracking?
Colour the grid like a chessboard. How can you sometimes answer 0 without searching at all?
